summary: Defines how SOAP messages, the XML-based messaging format used for remote procedure calls and notifications, are carried over BEEP, a framework for building application protocols. This binding describes how SOAP messages are transmitted across the network when BEEP is the underlying transport. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: SOAP is a way of wrapping a request in an XML envelope so that a program on another machine can read it. BEEP is a framing protocol that takes care of the messy part of putting such messages on a network: numbering them, splitting them into pieces, and telling the two ends apart. This document joins the two, and also defines two web addresses, soap.beep and soap.beeps, for naming a SOAP service carried this way.

subtitle: How to carry SOAP messages over BEEP, the framing protocol designed for building application protocols.

tldr.problem: SOAP says what a message looks like but not how to put it on the network. BEEP is a framing protocol built for exactly that job, but the two had never been joined up.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a BEEP profile for SOAP, a boot exchange that identifies the resource and negotiates features, and a mapping from the three SOAP message patterns onto BEEP's MSG, RPY, ANS and NUL messages.
tldr.outcome: This obsoletes RFC 3288 and adds support for the MTOM and XOP packaging technique, so that SOAP messages can carry attachments without base64 encoding them.

today: RFC 4227 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of the SOAP binding to BEEP. It replaced RFC 3288, and it was later updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: What This Document Specifies
sections.content:
The memo specifies a Simple Object Access Protocol binding to the BEEP core. A SOAP binding describes how SOAP messages are transmitted in the network.

SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol used to implement a wide variety of distributed messaging models. It defines a message format and describes a variety of message patterns, including but not limited to Remote Procedure Calling, asynchronous event notification, unacknowledged messages, and forwarding via SOAP intermediaries.

Conforming implementations MUST support SOAP version 1.2 and MAY support other versions, such as SOAP version 1.1. Unlike its predecessor, RFC 3288, the memo does not mandate the use of SOAP version 1.1. Throughout the memo, the term envelope refers to the top-level element exchanged by SOAP senders and receivers, and the terms peer, client, server, one-to-one and one-to-many are used in the context of BEEP.
sections.plainLanguage: SOAP is the message; BEEP is the envelope it travels in. This document says exactly how a SOAP message is placed inside BEEP's framing, so that two programs can talk to each other without either of them knowing anything about the other's network.

sections.title: The Profile and Its Two States
sections.content:
The BEEP profile for SOAP is identified as http://iana.org/beep/soap/VERSION in the BEEP profile element during channel creation, where VERSION refers to the numeric version of the SOAP specification. For example, http://iana.org/beep/soap/1.2 refers to version 1.2. RFC 3288 used http://iana.org/beep/soap for profile identification for SOAP version 1.1 envelopes, so an implementation that chooses to implement SOAP 1.1 should support both that URI and http://iana.org/beep/soap/1.1.

In BEEP, when the first channel is successfully created, the serverName attribute in the start element identifies the virtual host associated with the peer acting in the server role. The serverName attribute is analogous to HTTP's Host request-header field.

There are two states in the BEEP profile for SOAP, boot and ready. In the boot state, the peer requesting the creation of the channel sends a bootmsg, either during channel initialization or in a MSG message. If the other peer sends a bootrpy, then the ready state is entered. Otherwise the other peer sends an error, and no state change occurs. In the ready state, either peer begins a SOAP message pattern by sending a MSG message containing an envelope. The other peer completes the message pattern either by sending back an RPY message containing an envelope, or by sending back zero or more ANS messages, each containing an envelope, followed by a NUL message. Regardless, no state change occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: A BEEP channel for SOAP starts in a kind of waiting room where the two ends sort out which service is being used and what optional features they both understand. Once that is done the channel is ready and the actual messages flow.

sections.title: Profile Initialization and the Boot Message
sections.content:
The boot message is used for two purposes: resource identification, since each channel bound to the BEEP profile for SOAP provides access to a single resource, a network data object or service; and feature negotiation, so that if new features of SOAP emerge, their use can be negotiated.

The boot message contains a mandatory resource attribute, which is analogous to HTTP's abs_path Request-URI parameter, and an optional features attribute, which if present contains one or more feature tokens, each indicating an optional feature of the BEEP profile for SOAP that is being requested for possible use over the channel. If the peer acting in the server role recognizes the requested resource, it replies with the boot response, which contains one optional features attribute holding a subset of the feature tokens in the boot message, indicating which features may be used over the channel. If not present or empty, no features may be used.

Otherwise, if the boot message is improperly formed or if the requested resource is not recognized, the peer acting in the server role replies with an error message. Typically the boot message and its response are exchanged during channel initialization, but the channel remains in the boot state after an unsuccessful exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The boot exchange does two jobs at once: it names the service the client wants, and it lets the two ends agree on optional extras. If the server does not recognise the name, it says so and the channel stays unusable.

sections.title: SOAP Message Packages
sections.content:
The BEEP profile for SOAP transmits envelopes encoded as UTF-8 and SHOULD use the media type application/soap+xml. To provide compatibility with RFC 3288, it MAY use the media type application/xml.

In addition, an implementation of the BEEP profile for SOAP MAY support transmission of envelopes using the MTOM and XOP packaging technique, which sends a MIME multipart body whose parts are referenced from the XML rather than embedded in it. Because BEEP provides an 8-bit-wide path, a transformative Content-Transfer-Encoding such as base64 or quoted-printable should not be used. When an implementation of BEEP in SOAP does support MTOM and XOP, it SHOULD support the MIME Multipart/Related XOP Package format, and MAY support others. Additional formats could in the future include XOP package formats specific to BEEP, for example sending the attachments on a different channel to the SOAP channel, which would avoid searching for the MIME boundary tags and allows lazy delivery of attachments, delivering them only when really needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinarily the whole SOAP message, attachments and all, is one XML document in UTF-8. The optional packaging technique splits the attachments out into separate parts and points at them from the XML, so large binary files are not wasted through a text encoding.

sections.title: SOAP Message Patterns
sections.content:
A one-way message involves sending a message without any response being returned. The BEEP profile for SOAP achieves this using a one-to-many exchange, in which the client sends a MSG message containing an envelope, and the server immediately sends back a NUL message, before processing the contents of the envelope.

A request and response exchange involves sending a request, which results in a response being returned. The BEEP profile for SOAP achieves this using a one-to-one exchange, in which the client sends a MSG message containing an envelope, and the server sends back an RPY message containing an envelope.

A request and N-responses exchange involves sending a request, which results in zero or more responses being returned. The BEEP profile for SOAP achieves this using a one-to-many exchange, in which the client sends a MSG message containing an envelope, and the server sends back zero or more ANS messages, each containing an envelope, followed by a NUL message.

For error handling, the BEEP profile for SOAP does not use the ERR message for SOAP faults. When performing one-to-one exchanges, whatever SOAP response, including SOAP faults, generated by the server is always returned in the RPY message. When performing one-to-many exchanges, whatever SOAP response, including SOAP faults, generated by the server is always returned in the ANS messages. If there is an error with the BEEP message unrelated to the SOAP envelope, for example a poorly formed MIME message or an unsupported MIME Content-Type, then the server responds with an ERR message with an appropriate reply code.
sections.plainLanguage: Three shapes of conversation map onto BEEP's messages. A question and an answer is one MSG and one RPY. A question with several answers is one MSG, then any number of ANS, then a NUL to say that is all. A SOAP-level error is not an error at this level; it comes back as an ordinary reply.

sections.title: The Requesting and Responding State Machines
sections.content:
For binding instances conforming to the specification, a SOAP node instantiated at the BEEP peer that initiates the message exchange may assume the role of RequestingSOAPNode, and a SOAP node instantiated at the other BEEP peer may assume the role of RespondingSOAPNode.

The requesting node starts in the Init state, where a BEEP message is formulated and transmission begins, and then the state changes to Requesting. In the Requesting state more of the request message is transmitted and the arrival of the response is awaited. When the beginning of the response message is received, if it is a BEEP ERR message then the state transitions to Fail; otherwise the state transitions to Sending and Receiving. In that state the transmission of the request message and the receiving of the response message are completed, and once the receipt of the response is completed the state transitions to Success. Success and Fail are the terminal states of the machine.

The responding node starts in Init, where it awaits the start of the inbound request and may only generate ERR messages. It then moves to Receiving, where it begins to receive the request message and prepares the start of the response, and then to Receiving and Sending, where the receiving of the request and the sending of the response are completed before the transition to the Success state. Success and Fail are the terminal states that indicate completion of the message exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The document spells out the steps each side goes through, so that a slow reply cannot deadlock a sender that is still streaming its request. The requesting side must be able to read the beginning of the answer while it is still writing the question.

sections.title: The soap.beep and soap.beeps URL Schemes
sections.content:
The memo defines two URL schemes, soap.beep and soap.beeps, which identify the use of SOAP over BEEP over TCP. The soap.beep URL scheme uses the generic URI syntax: the value soap.beep is used for the scheme component and the server-based naming authority is used for the authority component. The path component maps to the resource component of the boot message sent during profile initialization, and if absent it defaults to a single slash. The values of both the scheme and authority components are case-insensitive.

The soap.beep URL scheme indicates the use of the BEEP profile for SOAP running over TCP/IP. If the authority component contains a domain name and a port number, then the DNS is queried for the A resource records corresponding to the domain name and the port number is used directly. If the authority contains a domain name and no port number, the Service Record algorithm is used with a service parameter of soap-beep and a protocol parameter of tcp; if no appropriate SRV records are found, the DNS is queried for the A records and the port number assigned by IANA is used. If the authority contains an IP address, the DNS is not queried and the address is used directly, with the port taken from the URL or from the IANA assignment.

The soap.beeps URL scheme is identical in all ways to the soap.beep URL scheme, with the exception that prior to starting the BEEP profile for SOAP the BEEP session must be tuned for privacy. Both URL schemes use the identical algorithms and parameters for address resolution. There are two ways to perform privacy tuning on a BEEP session: a transport security profile may be successfully started, or a user authentication profile that supports transport security may be successfully started. Upon completion of the negotiation, a tuning reset occurs in which both BEEP peers issue a new greeting.
sections.plainLanguage: A soap.beep address names a SOAP service: the host part says where to connect and the path part says which service to ask for. The soap.beeps form is the same, except that the connection must be made private first, so the two ends negotiate encryption before saying anything else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Although service provisioning is a policy matter, at a minimum all implementations MUST provide the following tuning profiles: for authentication, http://iana.org/beep/SASL/DIGEST-MD5; for confidentiality, http://iana.org/beep/TLS using the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher; and for both, http://iana.org/beep/TLS using the same cipher but supporting client-side certificates.

Furthermore, implementations may choose to offer MIME-based security services providing message integrity and confidentiality, such as OpenPGP or S/MIME. Regardless, the BEEP core specification's Section 9 holds a discussion of BEEP-specific security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation has to offer at least one way to authenticate the peer and one way to encrypt the session. It may also protect the messages themselves, for instance with S/MIME, on top of the protection of the channel.

viz.caption: THE TWO STATES OF A BEEP CHANNEL FOR SOAP
THE BEEP MESSAGES THAT CARRY SOAP ENVELOPES

messages.label: MSG
messages.note: The client sends a SOAP envelope.

messages.label: RPY
messages.note: One-to-one exchange: the answer comes back in a reply.

messages.label: ANS
messages.note: One-to-many exchange: zero or more answers, each carrying an envelope.

messages.label: NUL
messages.note: The NUL message ends the one-to-many exchange.

viz.caption: A SOAP ENVELOPE CARRIED IN A BEEP MSG MESSAGE

data.title: MSG with a SOAP envelope
data.code:
MSG 1 1 . 0 284
Content-Type: application/soap+xml

<env:Envelope
     xmlns:env="http://www.w3.org/2003/05/soap-envelope">
  <env:Header>
   <m:GetLastTradePrice xmlns:m="Some-URI" />
  </env:Header>
  <env:Body>
    <symbol xmlns:p="Some-URI" >DIS</symbol>
  </env:Body>
</env:Envelope>
END

items.title: soap.beep
items.text: Identifies a SOAP resource reached with the BEEP profile for SOAP over TCP/IP.

items.title: soap.beeps
items.text: Identical, except that the BEEP session must first be tuned for privacy.

items.title: The path
items.text: Maps to the resource component of the boot message, and defaults to a single slash if absent.

items.title: Finding the address
items.text: A port number in the URL is used directly; otherwise the DNS SRV record with the service name soap-beep is looked up, then the IANA-assigned port.

viz.caption: THE TUNING PROFILES EVERY IMPLEMENTATION MUST OFFER

items.title: Authentication
items.text: The tuning profile http://iana.org/beep/SASL/DIGEST-MD5 must be provided.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: The tuning profile http://iana.org/beep/TLS must be provided, using the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher.

items.title: Both
items.text: The same TLS profile, but supporting client-side certificates.

items.title: Message-level security
items.text: Implementations may also offer MIME-based services such as OpenPGP or S/MIME.
